blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Scalable and private media consumption with Popcorn' by Gupta et al. (2016), which explores how to provide privacy-preserving streaming media services where even the service provider cannot determine what media a user is consuming. The author highlights that Popcorn achieves this privacy at a cost of approximately 3.87x the baseline non-private service, with significant computational and I/O overheads that are manageable due to the low cost of CPU resources. The paper introduces a blend of Computational Private Information Retrieval (CPIR) and Information-Theoretic Private Information Retrieval (ITPIR) techniques to make privacy practical at scale. The key insight is combining these PIR methods to balance computational costs and content distribution concerns while addressing real-time streaming constraints and variable media object sizes.
paper_title: Scalable and private media consumption with Popcorn
paper_abstract: We describe the design, implementation, and evaluation of Popcorn, a media delivery system that hides clients’ consumption (even from the content distributor). Popcorn relies on a powerful cryptographic primitive: private information retrieval (PIR). With novel refinements that leverage the properties of PIR protocols and media streaming, Popcorn scales to the size of Netflix’s library (8000 movies) and respects current controls on media dissemination. The dollar cost to serve a media object in Popcorn is 3.87× that of a non-private system.
